lesson.title: Great results come from a few hits, not consistency
lesson.author_argues: Morgan Housel argues that no one makes good decisions all the time, and that even the most impressive people are full of bad ideas they act on. He says role models' gains come from a small share of their actions, so our own failures do not mean we are doing something wrong.
lesson.principle: Outcomes are driven by a small number of outsized wins, so a high miss rate is normal and only fatal if the misses are large and the hits are not.
lesson.evidence: The most impressive people are packed full of horrendous ideas that are often acted upon.
lesson.caveat: They may have been more right when they were right, but they could have been wrong just as often as you.
lesson.short_quote: no one makes good decisions all the time
lesson.applies_when: A founder is judging their own portfolio of bets, features, hires or experiments and feels like a failure because most of them did not work.
example_questions: Six of my last eight experiments flopped; am I bad at this?
How many failed bets should I expect before one works?
Should I stop launching things that might fail?

good.why: One distinct idea (tail-driven results), with a real caveat from the second paragraph and an applicable trigger for a founder.

lesson.title: Summarize their view until they say 'that's right'
lesson.author_argues: Chris Voss recounts a hostage negotiation in which the Philippine negotiator Benjie, after months of deadlock, mirrored, labeled and summarized Abu Sabaya's grievances. Sabaya answered 'That's right' and dropped his war-damages demand. Voss argues that this response marks a point where the other side agrees without feeling they gave in.
lesson.principle: Fully restating the other side's position and the emotion behind it, in your own words, makes them confirm it themselves, which removes the barrier to moving forward.
lesson.evidence: It created a realization point with our adversary where he actually agreed on a point without the feeling of having given in.
lesson.short_quote: agreed on a point without the feeling of having given in
lesson.applies_when: A founder is stuck in a deadlock with a customer, investor, cofounder or partner who keeps repeating the same demand despite logical arguments.
example_questions: My cofounder keeps rejecting my plan no matter what data I show; what do I try?
A customer insists on a discount I cannot give; how do I move them?
How do I stop arguing in circles with an investor?

good.why: Story-based, complete arc (tactic, outcome, mechanism), and the principle is transferable to a founder deadlock.

lesson.title: Baseline, tune, then pivot or persevere
lesson.author_argues: Eric Ries argues that startups should repeat a rhythm: establish the baseline, tune the engine, and make a decision to pivot or persevere. Poor quantitative results create the motivation for qualitative research that produces new hypotheses. He says optimization only pays off if the startup is building the right thing.
lesson.principle: Measure where you are, run improvements against that baseline, and if the numbers do not move, treat that as evidence the plan may be wrong rather than as a reason to work harder.
lesson.evidence: If you are building the wrong thing, optimizing the product or its marketing will not yield significant results.
lesson.caveat: As long as we are executing the plan well, hard work yields results.
lesson.short_quote: establish the baseline, tune the engine, and make a decision to pivot or persevere
lesson.applies_when: A founder keeps shipping improvements and working harder, but a core metric such as conversion or retention has not moved for months.
example_questions: We ship every week but sign-ups to paid is flat; do I push harder?
How do I know when to pivot versus keep improving?
What should I measure before changing the product again?

good.why: A named, repeatable three-step loop with a decision rule and a verbatim caveat limiting where optimization works.

lesson.title: Controlling your time is the highest dividend
lesson.author_argues: Morgan Housel argues that controlling your time is the highest dividend money pays. He cites elderly Americans who valued friendships and time with their children.
lesson.principle: Controlling your time is the most valuable thing money buys.
lesson.evidence: Take it from those who have lived through everything: Controlling your time is the highest dividend money pays.
lesson.short_quote: Controlling your time is the highest dividend money pays.
lesson.applies_when: A founder thinks about money and happiness.
example_questions: Should I value my time more?
How do I be happier as a founder?

bad.why: A slogan: the principle restates the quote with no mechanism, no action and no trigger, and the questions are generic enough for any person.

lesson.title: Track customer flows and avoid success theater
lesson.author_argues: Eric Ries argues that every company depends on customer flows, which allow a quantitative understanding of the business. He also says that vanity metrics tempt managers into success theater such as last-minute ad buys and channel stuffing.
lesson.principle: Measure customer flows through funnels and cohorts, and avoid vanity metrics so you do not resort to success theater.
lesson.evidence: Customer flows govern the interaction of customers with a company’s products.
lesson.applies_when: A founder reviews metrics and also feels pressure to look good for the board.
example_questions: Which metrics should I show my board?
How do I build a funnel for my product?
Why are my total user numbers misleading?

bad.why: Fuses two ideas (funnel and flow analysis, and vanity metrics driving success theater) that need separate lessons and separate applies_when.

lesson.title: Concentrate your bets on ten winners like Buffett
lesson.author_argues: Charlie Munger argues that Berkshire should hold only about ten stocks, since Warren Buffett made most of his money on 10 of 400 to 500. Munger says founders should therefore run a concentrated portfolio of bets.
lesson.principle: Pick roughly ten bets and concentrate everything on them, because that is how Buffett and Munger built Berkshire.
lesson.evidence: At the Berkshire Hathaway shareholder meeting in 2013 Warren Buffett said he’s owned 400 to 500 stocks during his life and made most of his money on 10 of them.
lesson.applies_when: A founder is deciding how many projects to run at once.
example_questions: How many projects should I run at once?
Should I focus on ten things?

bad.why: Misattributed and ungrounded: the cited text says Buffett owned 400 to 500 stocks and Munger said removing a few top investments makes the record average, not that anyone should hold ten; Munger never argues for ten-bet concentration here.
